summary: Kurt Huber worked in philosophy and other fields. After attending Eberhard-Ludwigs-Gymnasium, he earned his PhD at the University of Munich (~1913–1917), where he later served as außerordentlicher Professor (1926) and held a professorship (1938).

Kurt Tropper specializes in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He earned his doctorate at the University of Vienna by 2001 under Ernst Steinkellner, also studying under Michael Torsten Much and Tashi Geisler, and held posts at Vienna and the Austrian Academy of Sciences.

Kurtis R. Schaeffer specializes in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. After degrees at Lewis & Clark, Evergreen State, Washington (under Collett Cox and Richard G. Salomon), and Harvard (under Leonard van der Kuijp), he taught at Alabama and the University of Virginia.
Kurunegoda Piyatissa was a scholar in Buddhist studies and Indology. He was attested as head of the New York Buddhist Vihara in 1998, with his affiliation there attested again in 2009.

Kwangsoo Park works in Buddhist studies and religious studies. He earned an MA from the University of Iowa and a PhD from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, later serving as a professor at Wonkwang University (attested 2020).

Kyo Kano works in Indology and philosophy. After studying at Keio University, Kyoto University, and the University of Vienna, he was an assistant at Kyoto University (attested 1989) and an associate professor at Kobe Women's University (attested 2000).

Kyojun Shimizutani worked in Buddhist studies, studying under Keijun Shimizutani and at Tendai Sect University and Taisho University. He served as professor at Tendai Sect University and Taisho University, principal of Hieizan High School, and abbot of Senso-ji (~1974–1979).

Kyoko Fujii works in Buddhist studies and Indology. After studying at the University of Tokyo (~1968–1978), she was a professor at Yokohama City, Hamamatsu, Hokkaido, and ICPBS, and became director of the International Institute for Buddhist Studies (attested 2020–2026).
Kyoko Tokuno works in Buddhist studies and Sinology. She held positions at the University of Oregon and the University of Washington, where she was attested as a professor in 2017.
Kyokuga Saeki was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied under numerous traditional teachers, including Reiga and Gen'yū. He served as the 143rd abbot of Sennyu-ji.

Kyosho Hayashima worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He held academic posts as a lecturer at Yokohama City University (1962), assistant professor at Toyo University (1962), and professor at the University of Tokyo (1980).
Kyosho Tanaka is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1966–1974). He served as an associate professor at Musashino University from ~1976 to 2017.
Kyoshun Todo was a Buddhist studies scholar. He held academic appointments at Bukkyo University, serving as an assistant professor (attested 1962) and later as a professor (attested 1988–1992).

Kyozo Yamada was a Buddhist studies and religious studies figure. Educated at the First Higher School and Tokyo Imperial University, he studied under several traditional teachers, founded Kamakura Haku-un-kai, and became the second head of Sanbo Zen in 1970.

Kyōtarō Nishikawa worked in history, archaeology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Keio University (~1949–1953), he served as Director-General of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties (~1990–1996) and held a post at Kanagawa Prefectural Museum (~1996–2012).

Kōgi Kudara was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He served as a professor at Ryukoku University (~1978–2004) and was an editor for the Ryukoku Buddhist Society (attested 2002).
Kōichi Kozaka works in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied under Hakuyu Hadano and served as a professor at Osaka Kyoiku University (attested 1991).

Kōsen Imakita was a Buddhist studies and philosophy figure. He studied under Togai Fujisawa, Kyokuso Hirose, Daisetsu Jōen, and Gisan Zenkai, and served as abbot of Eikō-ji (1858) and Engaku-ji (1875–1892).
Kōshō Ōtani was a Buddhist studies figure who succeeded Kozui Otani. He studied at the First Higher School (~1929–1932) and Tokyo Imperial University (~1932–1935).

L. P. N. Perera worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He held posts as a supervisor at Vidyodaya Campus, University of Sri Lanka, and as Director of the Postgraduate Institute of Pali and Buddhist Studies.
